walkthroughs.body_html:
The royal court had around 1,000 people.

It travelled between palaces like Whitehall, Greenwich and Hampton Court. Courtiers competed for the queen's attention — and the patronage she could give. Style, dance and witty talk mattered hugely.

Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was Elizabeth's lifelong favourite — possibly even her love.

Later came Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex. He grew arrogant, led a failed rebellion in 1601 and was executed. Elizabeth was said to mourn him deeply.

Elizabeth ruled with her Privy Council, Parliament and JPs.

Each summer she went on 'progress' — visiting nobles' houses to be seen by her people. It saved money and let her show off her power. Hosting Elizabeth was costly but a great honour.

mcqs.q: In what year was the Earl of Essex executed for rebellion?
What was the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559?
options: Elizabeth reunited England with the Pope to make peace with Spain.
Elizabeth made England fully Protestant and banned Catholic worship outright.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
A deliberate via media — a Protestant doctrine and English-language prayer book combined with some Catholic-style ceremony — designed to maximise conformity.

mcqs.q: Why was the Spanish Armada defeated in 1588?
options: Drake defeated the Armada single-handedly in a great sea battle.
A combination of English tactics and fireships, poor Spanish planning, and the 'Protestant wind' storms that wrecked the fleet on the return.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
Elizabeth I personally commanded the English fleet at sea.

mcqs.q: Why did William of Normandy claim the English throne in 1066?
options: William invaded because he was the strongest king in Europe and wanted more land.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
He claimed Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne in 1051 and that Harold Godwinson had sworn an oath to support that claim in 1064.
Elizabeth I personally commanded the English fleet at sea.
